findings.statement: CA9 is the top-ranked convergence gene and the literature supports it as a diagnostic imaging biomarker. PMID:42473996 reports that CA9 is preferentially enriched in ccRCC tumor cells with low background expression in normal kidney, that CA9-targeted PET gives proof-of-concept noninvasive discrimination of ccRCC 'warranting prospective validation', and that high uptake is associated with PBRM1 loss-of-function. This is a single proof-of-concept imaging study, not a validated clinical biomarker. PMID:35795483 also reports CAIX mRNA increased in HIV-associated kidney cancer. CA9 is not a prognostic marker in the data profile.

CD70 is supported as a therapeutic and imaging target. PMID:38195301 states CD70 is commonly overexpressed in RCC and minimally expressed in normal tissue, 'making it a potential therapeutic target', and that in ccRCC it correlates with hypoxia pathway proteins and is a downstream target of HIF. PMID:39510586 reports high and specific expression in ccRCC, two CD70-specific single-domain antibodies (RCCB3, RCCB6) labelled with 68Ga as radiotracers, and an association of CD70 with overall survival. Evidence is preclinical or tracer development; the omics and tractability layers (CD70-directed agents are in early-phase trials) agree with it.

NNMT is upregulated in ccRCC tumor tissue and high expression correlates with worse overall and disease-specific survival (P < 0.001) in PMID:41399267, which concludes it is a 'promising prognostic biomarker and potential therapeutic target' with transcriptomic, clinical and functional validation. Potent selective NNMT inhibitors (II559, II802) exist (PMID:37523719), but this chemistry paper is not ccRCC-specific. NNMT is also high in the data-only target and biomarker profiles, so literature and omics agree; no NNMT inhibitor is approved.

ALDOB is down in ccRCC (IHC lower than adjacent normal; PMID:40852386) and is presented as a prognostic biomarker and potential immunotherapy target in PMID:40852386 and PMID:38655323 ('independent predictor of prognosis in KIRC'). It correlates with infiltrating Treg, Th17 cells and neutrophils. The support is bioinformatic plus IHC in a few studies. A pan-cancer paper (PMID:37083815) reports low expression across cancers, so it is not ccRCC-specific. Downregulated genes are better framed as biomarkers than as drug targets, which the data target profile reflects.

ENO2 has the most extensive literature among the upregulated metabolic genes. PMID:37760940 reports ENO2 as a potential diagnostic biomarker that independently predicts prognosis and promotes ccRCC progression via the Warburg effect. PMID:39091581 reports high ENO2 in ccRCC cell lines, and knockdown inhibits glycolysis, promotes ferroptosis and affects mitochondrial function. PMID:36313709 links ENO2 to overall survival. This is mechanistic in vitro work plus database analyses; no in vivo or clinical validation is in the corpus and no ENO2 drug is listed.

COXFA4L2 (NDUFA4L2) has the densest mechanistic literature. It is HIF-driven (PMID:42331208, PMID:36722045), over 90% of ccRCCs overexpress it, and it raises glycolysis. PMID:34970493 reports it predicts poor survival, supports proliferation and enhances CA9 expression in an early-ccRCC mouse model. PMID:42331208 reports it suppresses mitochondria-associated ferroptosis cooperatively with LDHB, and that targeting the NDUFA4L2/LDHB axis is promising, particularly with radiotherapy. It also appears as a tissue and extracellular-vesicle marker of low- and high-grade ccRCC (PMID:41656939). Evidence is preclinical; note it has no TCGA replication record in the ranking row.

MT1G is lower in ccRCC tissue than normal (PMID:36204178), yet the literature is partly contradictory about its role. PMID:36204178 calls it a negative regulator of ferroptosis and a poor-prognosis biomarker. PMID:38906969 reports that low MT1G in tissue but high MT1G correlates with advanced stage and poorer prognosis, and that elevated MT1G promotes growth and metastasis in vitro and in vivo by inhibiting CPT1B and increasing lipid droplets. So it is lost in tumors but oncogenic when high within tumors; it should not be treated as a simple tumor-suppressor target.

ABAT is underexpressed in KIRC among 11 cancers (PMID:41158242). The same paper says it predicted poor prognosis in KIRC, which is the opposite direction to what loss of expression would suggest; the sentence is ambiguous and the data layers should be checked. PMID:41813748 reports ABAT overexpression suppresses tumor growth in vitro and in vivo, mediated through cGAS-STING and PRMT5 with enhanced interferon signaling. Evidence is bioinformatic with some functional work. The listed drug vigabatrin is an ABAT inhibitor, which is the wrong direction if ABAT is tumor-suppressive.

FCER1G is upregulated in ccRCC tissue and relates to macrophage infiltration, T cell suppression and unfavourable prognosis (PMID:35120484). It showed prognostic importance in patients treated with nivolumab but not everolimus, and combined with CD68 may serve as a postoperative prognostic index. This is one bioinformatic study. Because the signal is immune-cell derived, it is a tumor-microenvironment marker rather than a tumor-intrinsic target.

PFKP is upregulated in kidney cancer, especially ccRCC (PMID:34321910), and is among the most consistently upregulated genes with PLIN2, PLOD2, VEGFA, CCND1 and IGFBP3 (PMID:36901940). PMID:40341002 lists PFKP among glycolysis-related biomarkers with diagnostic and prognostic potential. A contradiction exists: PMID:34321910 reports that low PFKP expression correlated with poor 5-year and 10-year overall survival, despite upregulation in tumors. Evidence is bioinformatic.

PLIN2 is among consistently upregulated ccRCC genes (PMID:36901940). PMID:34482820 reports its diagnostic potential for renal neoplasms, validated by immunohistochemistry on tissue micro-arrays with 128 samples. PMID:35314744 relates PLIN2 expression to prognosis from database survival analysis. It fits the lipid-droplet phenotype of ccRCC; evidence for diagnostic use is modest and is not about targeting.

SLC22A8 is lower in ccRCC at protein, phosphoprotein and DNA methylation level than normal tissue, low methylation predicted poor overall survival, and it correlates with survival and immune infiltration (PMID:36123895), which proposes it as a prognostic biomarker. This is a single multi-omic bioinformatic study. It is also high in the data biomarker profile (prognosis), so the two agree. The downregulated transporter is a marker of proximal tubule identity, not a plausible drug target in tumor cells.

UMOD is reported as downregulated in ccRCC across several independent expression studies (PMID:36899967, PMID:37275334) and in HIV-associated kidney cancer (PMID:35795483), consistent with loss of normal nephron identity. The corpus offers no prognostic or functional claim for UMOD, so it is a tissue-of-origin marker rather than an actionable gene.

Chunks from PMID:42422841 state that VHL inactivation leads to HIF-2alpha accumulation, which activates pathways that promote tumor growth, and that the HIF-2alpha inhibitor belzutifan has been FDA-approved for ccRCC. This is the only validated clinical targeting route in the corpus and ties together the HIF-driven genes (CA9, CD70, NDUFA4L2). No literature relations are extracted for VHL or EPAS1 as genes (n_literature_relations is 0), despite strong Open Targets and genetic support, so their role rests on Open Targets and review chunks.

caveats: SCARB1, PIGR, SLC12A1, SLC47A2, PAH, ENPP3, AQP2, FGF1, SLC5A2, SLC13A3, SLC36A2, ENPP6, CASR, DPEP1, VHL, EPAS1 and TP53 have strong omics and/or Open Targets support but zero ccRCC literature relations in this corpus (a search for SCARB1/PIGR/ENPP3 returned only irrelevant sentences). Their absence reflects corpus coverage, not evidence against them.

Many literature claims are single-study TCGA/GEO bioinformatic signatures (ALDOB, ABAT, FCER1G, PFKP, SLC22A8) without prospective validation. Only belzutifan (HIF-2alpha) is an approved ccRCC-specific targeted route in this corpus; CA9 PET is explicitly proof-of-concept.

Contradictions: MT1G is low in tumors yet high expression predicts poor outcome and promotes growth; PFKP is up in tumors but low PFKP was linked to poor survival in one study; the ABAT prognosis sentence is ambiguous relative to its downregulation; FABP1 literature in the corpus concerns colorectal cancer and lung adenocarcinoma discrimination, not ccRCC, so it gives no ccRCC support.

Many top-ranked genes are downregulated kidney-identity genes (ALDOB, SLC22A8, UMOD, FABP1, NPHS2); these suit biomarker use but not therapeutic inhibition. DepMap selectivity is near zero for most candidates, so no gene shows tumor-cell dependency support for targeting.
